intro: You have reached Carchemish, an ancient city in Gaziantep province, its story running from the 3rd millennium BC to the 7th century BC. This was a royal city on the Euphrates, famed for its Hittite and Neo-Hittite reliefs.
history: It all began at a crossing of the Euphrates. Here the city was founded, and under Mitanni, the Hittites and the Neo-Hittites it served as a regional capital. In 605 BC the Battle of Carchemish brought Assyria to its end. Much later, in 1911–14, Leonard Woolley excavated the site.
structure-1: You are now looking at the Long Wall reliefs: stone slabs carved in relief that once adorned the Long Wall of Carchemish. Take a moment with them.
structure-2: Here is the Inner Gate, the inner defensive gateway of the city. Imagine the guards who once watched over this passage.
structure-4: Now to the Assyrian inscriptions. These cuneiform texts recount the campaigns and conquests of the Assyrian kings — history told in the conquerors' own words.
structure-5: And here is the Hittite Palace, a palace building dating to the Hittite period. Pause and picture the court that once filled it.
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the Royal Road.
facts: Did you know? Carchemish straddles today's Turkish-Syrian border. Part of the mound lies inside a military zone, and because the site was mined, it could not be dug for years. The city's Neo-Hittite reliefs form the backbone of the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations in Ankara. And T. E. Lawrence — Lawrence of Arabia — worked here as a young archaeologist on the 1911-14 excavations.
outro: This brings our tour of Carchemish to an end. Please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. Thank you for listening, and enjoy your visit.
